entries.title: divide a range of work across threads
entries.body:
* docs(plan): propose a compatibility dialect, and what `async` means in each

WP28 is the plan of record for a mode that accepts ordinary statically typed
TypeScript, so that a codebase is ported first and made fast afterwards one
construct at a time, and for the two lowerings of `async` that follow from it.

The useful half is the line that decides what may enter such a dialect, because
it is not "how hard is this to compile" but **can the compiler still name the
layout of every value**. If it can, the construct costs a proof — an attribute
the whole-program fixpoint was making, an allocation that goes back to the
arena — and the cost is measurable, local, and reportable through the
`performance` class WP15 item 2 already built, so the migration dashboard needs
no new machinery. If it cannot — `any`, an undeclared property, `Proxy`, a
prototype — the construct costs the object model: a tagged value, and a
collector for the boxes shortly after. That tier is refused in every dialect
permanently rather than staged.

Strict stays the default and does not grow, the mode may only *add* acceptance,
and the erasure invariant is a test rather than a promise: the corpus compiled
with the mode on emits byte-identical IR, and every `reject_*` case the
allow-list does not name still rejects with the same code and the same words.
The thesis is that the dialect is what lets strict stay small — wp23 declined
`?.`, a string `switch` and `for...of` over a string as language decisions,
correctly, and each is also code somebody has already written.

It forces the flag surface too. Twenty-three options across four axes with none
of them named in a spelling: the note regroups them into dialect / build /
output, gives the dialect one allow-list flag a team ratchets down in
package.json rather than twelve booleans, and records the dialect in the
emitted IR — which closes the older complaint that two modules from one source
under different `--number-mode` settings are different programs and neither
says so. It answers MASTER_PLAN §3.4's oldest open row on the way: `i32` in
strict, `f64` in compat, because a ported codebase that truncates at 2**31
diverges quietly.

On `async` it does not overturn wp24's refusal; it finds the one condition
under which the refusal does not apply, using wp24's own load-bearing finding.
wp24 §7 refuses erasure because it makes a program mean something different
under Node. wp24 §2 finds there is nothing to await — no timer, no sleep, no
poller, no socket, in either compiler or either runtime. Read the second
against the first and erasure is exact whenever no two promises are
simultaneously live, because a JavaScript `await` only reorders a program when
another pending continuation exists to run in the gap the yield opens. Two
checker rules imply it, and they are wp24 §9.3's "the promise as a value does
not survive" stated as a rule rather than a conclusion. `Promise.all` is the
case with two live promises and is admitted exactly when the fixpoint proves
the callees do not interfere — and that same proof lets the same expression
become a real fork and join under a second engine, `--async-model threads`,
riding WP20 T1 and T2. One analysis, two payoffs, and the second is parallelism
the single-threaded original could not have had.

Nothing is built and nothing adds a rule to LANGUAGE.md, so M4's freeze is not
waiting on this. The two measurements that could stop the package before it
start — what one indirect call costs the fixpoint whole-program, and how many
`async` functions in a real application ever await something that can block —
are named as spikes rather than predicted.

Refs: docs/wp24-async.md, docs/wp20-threads.md, docs/wp23-language-surface.md

* docs(runtime): measure the parallel payoff WP20 T4 was waiting on

wp20 §4 T4 and §7 both said the parallel win should be measured on a prototype
before T1's surface was designed. This is that measurement. Nothing in the
language spawns a thread, so the prototype is exactly what T0 made possible and
no more: three kernels compiled to the C ABI by the ordinary compiler, and a
pthreads driver that splits one fixed amount of work across T threads so that T
is the only variable. Four physical cores, no SMT, no cgroup quota; best of
five to nine per row with the thread counts interleaved.

A compute kernel returns **3.76x on four cores at 94% efficiency**, and 3.81x
netted against the binary a program would build today, because `--threads`
costs nothing at all when nothing touches the arena. That is the largest number
left anywhere in the plan — the WP15 list tops out at 2.48x for its one
remaining large item — so T1 and T2 are now worth building on a measurement
rather than on the soundness argument alone.

The second finding is the one the note did not expect and it changes what T4
has to be. **An allocating body's scaling is decided by its arena discipline,
not by the thread count.** The same loop returns 3.10x with the arena left to
grow and 1.86x once `Arena.reset()` recycles it every 4,096 objects — and the
recycling is worth 4.2x on its own, so the best configuration beats the naive
one by 6.4x of which only 1.5x is the threads. The cause is measured rather
than supposed: peak RSS is 1,432,228 KB against 1,828 KB for the same program,
so the unbounded version spends its time touching a gigabyte and a third of
memory it has never seen, and page-fault work divides reasonably well. Take
that away and what is left saturates at two threads. Part of the residual is
`malloc` contention over arena chunks and that part is measured too — the reset
interval moves 1.87x to 1.57x — but with the batch provably inside one chunk,
so that no `malloc` happens in the steady state, four threads still return
1.87x. That is named as unexplained rather than guessed at, with the kernel
that would separate it.

Four design inputs for T1 and T4 fall out, none of them a number: the
per-thread arena teardown already exists and needs no new runtime entry point,
`parallelFor` needs an arena story beside its partitioning story, `--threads`
should be implied by the language surface rather than requested beside it
because a program that never spawns should not pay the 1.10x-1.22x, and the
3.76x is what the runtime and the codegen allow rather than what a partitioned
nbody returns, which is still unmeasured.

Also records the sequencing decision that threads come before WP28's compat
`async`: that note's `--async-model threads` is this note's T1 and T2 wearing a
JavaScript spelling, and designing the engine through the notation would mean
designing T2's shareable-type rule through a keyword that hides it.

Measured: 3.76x on four cores (compute), 3.10x / 1.86x (allocating), 4.2x for
arena recycling alone
Refs: docs/wp20-threads.md#8-the-t4-payoff-measured

* docs(plan): price one opaque call, and settle compat's flag and sequencing

Three changes to WP28, all of them consequences of running the spike the note
named as able to stop the package.

**The flag is `--compat`**, bare for every built feature and `--compat=<list>`
for exactly some, with strict being the *absence* of the flag rather than a
value of it — so a strict build's command line does not change and neither does
its IR, which is what keeps the erasure invariant cheap to state. The dialect is
recorded as `!nish.compat` named metadata, absent for a strict build, so no
golden moves.

**S1 is measured, and it moved the headline.** One opaque callee in a hot loop,
three ways: wp27's `declare function`, which gives a genuinely attribute-less
callee inside the language as it is today; a hand-edited call through a pointer
the C half installs at run time, which gives a callee LTO cannot see either;
and `--no-stack-alloc`, which forbids the escape proof such a callee would take
away. The results, best of seven with the variants interleaved:

- The call itself is worth **1.26x** on a serial callback chain and **1.40x**
  with the same call inside an array loop. Real, survivable, roughly what a
  reader would guess.
- The frontend's own facts, in isolation, are worth **nothing**: 490 ms against
  489, and 542 against 543. Losing `readnone` and `willreturn` on every
  transitive caller cost zero, because the callee was still inside the LTO unit
  and LLVM re-derived what it needed. That is not a claim the fixpoint is
  worthless — WP15 §1a's alias facts are worth 1.63x to 3.96x — only that these
  facts, lost this way, are not what a closure charges.
- The escape proof is worth **8.76x**, and that is the whole story. Where an
  object is provably local today WP6 makes it an entry-block `alloca` and LLVM
  then removes it outright; an unknown callee cannot be given that proof, and
  200M arena bumps arrive. Nothing else in the note is within a factor of six.

The blast radius came out as predicted and is the only part that did: one
opaque leaf stripped facts from its entire transitive caller set, up to the
program entry, which is computable from the call graph the checker already
builds. So the cost is attributable — and what matters is the report's *order*,
because the three costs differ by a factor of six. The sample diagnostic now
leads with the object that moved to the arena and mentions the attribute loss
third, which is the reverse of what the note first guessed.

It also splits the closure stage along a line wp23 §6 had already drawn. A
callback whose callee is statically known — an arrow at the call site, a
function passed by name — is a direct call that inlines and keeps the escape
proof, and costs nothing; that is wp23's compile-time function parameter and it
covers most of what a migrating codebase spells with a callback. A function
value whose target the checker cannot name is the expensive one. They differ by
a factor of nine, the cheap half is built first, and a report that cannot tell a
user which of the two they wrote is not worth printing.

**Threads come before compat `async`.** `--async-model threads` is WP20's T1
and T2 wearing a JavaScript spelling, so the engine is built as `Thread.spawn`
/ `join` and a `parallelFor`, with its own surface and its own diagnostics,
before any `await` is lowered onto it. Designing it the other way round would
mean designing T2's shareable-type rule through a keyword that hides it.

MASTER_PLAN and the docs index carry both notes' new numbers, including WP20's
parallel measurement from the commit before this one.

Measured: 1.26x-1.40x for the call, nothing for the frontend facts, 8.76x for
the escape proof
Refs: docs/wp28-compatibility-mode.md#74-s1-measured--and-the-headline-it-moves

* docs(runtime): commit the thread surface, and test that it is legal TypeScript

wp20 left the surface open on purpose: "the stage that decides how much real
work is expressible, so it is the one to prototype against a real program
before committing to the surface". WP29 is that commitment, and the question it
turns on is narrower than the design question — given that a Nish program has
to be legal TypeScript, what is the best surface we can actually spell?

**TypeScript will not give us a keyword.** `go f()`, `spawn { }` and
`parallel for` are unsayable, so every construct has to be a call. The
exception is *lifetime*, and it is the find that shapes the whole design:
`using` (TS 5.2) is the one block-scoped deterministic-cleanup form the
language has, and a scoped thread group is exactly a block-scoped lifetime. So
the proposal takes Rust's shapes and Go's posture and lets the compiler supply
what both of them had to ask the programmer for:

- **Scoped threads spelled `using`.** wp20 T1's rule 2 — every handle joined on
  every path, proved with the CFG analysis behind `reject_missing_return` —
  becomes a join the compiler emits at every block exit. The rule is not
  proved, it is emitted, which deletes an analysis and the
  `reject_thread_unjoined` diagnostic and leaves one much simpler rule: a scope
  must be introduced by `using`. It also nests inside WP6's existing
  mark/release bracket rather than adding an invariant.
- **`Mutex<T>` owns the data it protects**, guard released by the block, so
  there is no unguarded path to the value. Buildable now: generic classes with
  methods already monomorphise.
- **Data parallelism as `parallelMapInto` / `parallelReduce`**, where the body
  is pure and the *intrinsic* performs every store — so disjointness is a
  property of the call rather than an obligation handed back to the programmer.
  `parallelFor` is deliberately not in the first stage for exactly that reason:
  a body that stores for itself makes "it writes only its own slot" a comment
  rather than a proof.
- **Race freedom from the fixpoint, not from annotations or a detector.** Rust
  asks for `Send`/`Sync`; Go ships a runtime detector and tolerates the bug
  until it fires. `attributes.ts` already proves `readnone`/`readonly` over the
  whole call graph, so a body it cannot clear is simply a compile error and the
  programmer writes nothing.

**Tested rather than asserted.** The declaration file and a program using every
construct go through `tsc --strict` at `"lib": ["ES2022"]`, exit 0, with no
tsconfig change required — because the shipped `.d.ts` declares the disposable
protocol itself instead of making consumers add `ESNext.Disposable`. Two costs
are named rather than hidden: that declaration file uses `declare global` and
`unique symbol`, both Phase 0 rejections, which is fine for a declaration the
compiler special-cases but should not be discovered by a reader; and `using`
today reaches the validator's `var` rule and is rejected with a message about
`var`, which would have to split.

The one thing the surface needs that does not exist is wp23 §6's compile-time
function parameter, for a body written at the call site — not function values,
and WP28 §7.4 measured a statically known callee at no run-time cost.

**It also argues for reversing wp20's stage order**, on wp20's own
measurement: data parallelism is where the entire payoff is *and* is the
smallest stage, needing no handle type, no join analysis, no handle-escape rule
and no capture rule. T4, T1, T3, with T2's shareable rule split between the
first two.

And one warning neither Rayon nor a `go` statement can give: the fixpoint knows
whether a parallel body allocates, and wp20 §8 measured what that costs, so the
compiler can say before the program runs that a region will be bound by memory
rather than by cores.

Refs: docs/wp29-thread-surface.md, docs/wp20-threads.md

* feat(runtime): divide a range of work across threads

`nish_parallel_range` is the stage under wp29's data-parallel surface, and the
first thing built of it. It has no language surface: nothing in the language
calls it yet, LANGUAGE.md does not move, and neither compiler changed.

    typedef void (*nish_par_body)(int64_t lo, int64_t hi, void *ctx);
    int64_t nish_cpu_count(void);
    void nish_parallel_range(nish_par_body body, void *ctx, int64_t len, int64_t grain);

It partitions `[0, len)` into contiguous chunks at most one element apart in
size, so no worker is the one everybody waits for; at most `nish_cpu_count()`
of them and never more than `len / grain`. Chunk 0 runs on the calling thread,
so N-way parallelism costs N-1 spawns and the caller is not idle while it
waits. A chunk whose thread could not be created runs on the calling thread
too, so running short of threads costs speed and never correctness. A body that
itself calls `nish_parallel_range` runs its range on one thread, because the
nesting guard is thread-local and there is no scheduler here: sequential
nesting is the conservative answer and the only one that needs no work
stealing.

It compiles in both configurations. Without `-DNISH_THREADS`, and on WASI where
there are no threads, the same entry point runs the whole range on the calling
thread — so the flag decides whether the work is divided, never whether the
function exists. Each worker frees its own arena before returning, which the
thread-local storage class of WP20 T0 makes a per-thread operation; the unit
test asserts the parent's arena comes through the join byte for byte, that
every index is visited exactly once, that the chunks partition the range with
no gap and no overlap, that exactly one chunk ran on the calling thread, that
every other chunk began with an empty arena, and that nesting does not multiply
the thread count.

**A third translation unit, for the reason the second one exists.**
`runtime_os.c` had 29 bytes of its ceiling left and this is 456; putting it
there would have raised the number a reader sees for "the operating-system
surface" for something whose subject is not a system call. So
`runtime_parallel.c` carries its own two ceilings — 26 bytes of `.text*` at
-Oz without the macro against a budget of 256, and 456 against 512 — and
`scripts/build.sh` pairs it with the `runtime.c` a caller names, as it already
pairs `runtime_os.c`, so no link line anywhere has to learn about it.

What it costs a program that does not use it is nothing, byte for byte:
`examples/hello.ts` at the size profile is 4,680 bytes with the file linked and
4,680 without, and `cmp` says the two binaries are identical.

**The payoff, re-measured through it** (four physical cores, one fixed amount of
work, best of five, one binary per row so the chunk count is the only
variable): a compute kernel 3.96x, an allocating one 3.09x, and the same
allocating one with its arena recycled 3.97x. Arena discipline is worth about
3x independently of the cores and three orders of magnitude of peak resident
memory — 1.37 GiB against 1.8 MB for the same source — so the two multipliers
compose to 12x against a naive single-threaded build.

**And it corrects the earlier measurement rather than folding it in.** wp20 §8
reported the recycled kernel at 1.86x on an ad-hoc pthreads driver, argued that
an allocating body's scaling collapses, and blamed part of it on arena chunk
churn with an interval sweep moving 1.87x to 1.57x. None of that holds: the
kernel scales 3.97x, the sweep is flat, and the limiter was the driver. Its
curve was non-monotonic — 243 ms at two threads and 246 at three — which should
have been read as a signal at the time, the new binary's sequential path is
slower rather than faster so this is not better inlining, and `-pthread`
accounts for about 8% of the gap. §8b keeps that visible. A prototype's
scaffolding is part of what it measures.

Measured: 3.96x / 3.09x / 3.97x on four cores; 12x combined with arena
discipline; 456 bytes of .text* at -Oz; hello.ts unchanged byte for byte
Refs: docs/wp20-threads.md, docs/wp29-thread-surface.md, docs/wp7-runtime.md
Tests: tests/runtime_test.c (both configurations), tests/run.js runtime-budget

* perf(runtime): cache the CPU count instead of asking on every region

`nish_cpu_count()` called `sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)` every time, and
`nish_parallel_range` calls it to decide how many chunks to make — so every
region paid for it, including the ones too small to divide, where it was the
entire cost. glibc answers that call from `sched_getaffinity` or by parsing
/sys/devices/system/cpu/online; measured here it is 3.7 us.

An empty region asking for one chunk — the undivided path, which takes no
thread at all — goes from **3,734 ns to 3 ns**. A region divided four ways goes
from about 137 us to about 125 us, where the rest is the three `pthread_create`
calls and their joins and is what dividing actually costs.

The number is cached in a word read and written with relaxed atomic builtins
rather than a plain `int64_t`: the race between two threads filling it is
benign, since both compute the same value, but it is still a race, and on
x86-64 the relaxed pair is a plain load and store. A machine whose online CPU
count changes under a running process therefore keeps the count it started
with, which is the right trade for a number that decides how many threads a
loop is divided into.

`.text*` at -Oz goes from 26 to 49 bytes without `-DNISH_THREADS` and from 456
to 482 with it, both inside the 256 and 512 byte ceilings, and
docs/wp7-runtime.md carries the new row.

wp20 §8e records what a region costs now that the measurement exists, because
it is the answer to a question the design keeps being asked: the threads are
the machine's, one per core, created and joined per region with no pool. An OS
thread here costs about forty times what a goroutine costs and there are at
most `nish_cpu_count()` of them by decision, so this divides one loop across
the cores and is not a way to have many tasks. A region needs on the order of a
millisecond of work inside it before the spawn is under a tenth of its cost,
which is the number wp29's P1 should pick its default `grain` from.

Measured: 3,734 ns -> 3 ns on the undivided path; ~125 us to divide four ways
Refs: docs/wp20-threads.md, docs/wp7-runtime.md
Tests: tests/runtime_test.c, tests/run.js runtime-budget
